name: South Sudan
summary: The world’s newest widely recognised country, independent from Sudan in 2011 after decades of civil war; a new civil war began in 2013.

knownFor.label: Sudd wetland
knownFor.note: One of the largest wetlands in the world.

knownFor.label: Cattle camps
knownFor.note: Herding at the heart of Dinka and Nuer life.

terrain.value: Savanna, the vast Sudd swamps along the White Nile, floodplains, and forested highlands in the south such as the Imatong Mountains.

climate.value: Tropical, with a wet season from about April to October and a hot dry season; heavy rains flood the Sudd and floodplains.

resources.value: Oil in the north, fertile farmland, timber, cattle and the water of the White Nile.

disasters.value: Severe floods in 2019–22 displaced hundreds of thousands; famine was declared in parts of the country in 2017.

population.value: About 12.7 million (an estimate; no census for decades).

urbanisation.value: Mostly rural; Juba, the capital, is the largest city, with smaller towns such as Wau and Malakal.

disease.value: Malaria, cholera, kala-azar and malnutrition are common; health care is very limited, especially outside towns.

economicBase.value: Oil (more than 90% of state revenue), herding.

tradeRoutes.value: Oil is exported by pipeline through Sudan to Port Sudan; other goods arrive by road from Kenya and Uganda.

wealth.value: One of the poorest countries in the world, despite its oil income.

inequality.value: Large gaps: a small elite controls oil money, while most people depend on farming, herding or aid.

governmentType.value: A federal presidential republic under a Transitional Constitution; the president is head of state, head of government and commander-in-chief.

keyRulers.value: South Sudan’s leaders since independence in 2011 are not named here. John Garang is not covered in the part read.

succession.value: Peace deals created power-sharing between the president and first vice-president; national elections have been repeatedly postponed.

institutions.value: A transitional government and a Transitional National Legislative Assembly set up under the 2018 peace agreement.

eliteConflict.value: Rivalry between the president and the former vice-president, partly along Dinka–Nuer lines.

armyAndTech.value: The army grew out of the SPLA rebel force and was renamed the South Sudan People’s Defence Forces in 2018.

majorWars.value: The Second Sudanese Civil War (1983–2005) ended with the Comprehensive Peace Agreement of 2005 (the page says more than 2 million died, and more than 2.5 million in the wars overall); the civil war from December 2013 killed about 400,000 and displaced over 4 million.

territoryChange.value: Abyei and other border areas disputed with Sudan.

alliancesRivals.value: Tense relations with Sudan over oil and borders, close ties with Uganda, and membership of the African Union and the East African Community.

inventions.value: No major inventions are associated with the modern state.

scienceEducation.value: Very low literacy, roughly a third of adults; the University of Juba is the main university.

openness.value: Limited by war and poor roads, though the country depends heavily on imports and foreign aid.

communicationTransport.value: Very few paved roads; barges use the White Nile, and the Juba–Nimule road links the capital to Uganda.

languageWriting.value: English (official); Dinka, Nuer and many others.

artsArchitecture.value: Beadwork, cattle songs and dances, scarification traditions among some groups, and round mud-and-thatch houses (tukuls).

socialStructure.value: More than 60 ethnic groups; the largest are the Dinka and Nuer, followed by the Zande, Bari, Shilluk and others.

sharedIdentity.value: Debated: the long struggle against Khartoum united many, but the civil war since 2013 deepened ethnic divisions.

dailyLife.value: Many families herd cattle and grow sorghum and maize, moving with the seasons; millions live in displacement camps.

neighbours.value: Sudan, Ethiopia, Kenya, Uganda, DR Congo, CAR.

ideasReligions.value: Christianity spread through missions from the 1800s and grew during the civil wars; traditional beliefs remain strong.

colonisation.value: Anglo-Egyptian Sudan (1899–1956), then part of Sudan.

peakPeriod.value: Too recent to judge; hopes were highest at independence in July 2011.

declineSignals.value: Civil war broke out in December 2013, less than three years after independence, causing mass displacement.

outcome.value: Still in existence as an independent republic with Juba as its capital.

overallCertainty.value: Basic facts are well documented; some figures are estimates.
